items.title: Section: Ten Grounds for Craving, Ten Matching Names — From Clinging to the Aggregates to Longing for Non-Existence

items.zh: 答：貪由十事生。一、取蘊，二、諸見，三、未得境界，四、已得境界，五、已所受用過去境界，六、惡行，七、男女，八、親友，九、資具，十、後有及無有。問：何貪於何事生耶？答：隨其次第，十貪於十事生。何等為十？謂事貪、見貪、貪貪、慳貪、蓋貪、惡行貪、子息貪、親友貪、資具貪、有無有貪。
items.en: Answer: craving arises from ten grounds — clinging to the aggregates, views, an unobtained object, an obtained object, a previously enjoyed object, unwholesome conduct, maleness and femaleness, friends and family, requisites, and future existence or non-existence. Correspondingly: craving for existent objects, craving for views, craving-craving, stingy craving, hindrance craving, craving for unwholesome conduct, craving for offspring, craving for friends, craving for requisites, and craving for existence or non-existence.

items.title: Section: Ten Grounds for Aversion, and the Nine Vexations That Surround Every Ordinary Life

items.zh: 瞋事亦有十種。一、己身，二、所愛有情，三、非所愛有情，四、過去怨親，五、未來怨親，六、現在怨親，七、不可意境，八、嫉妬，九、宿習，十、他見。瞋亦有十，如其次第，依彼而生。依前六事，立九惱事，緣彼一切瞋，皆名有情瞋；
items.en: The grounds of aversion are likewise ten: one's own body, a beloved being, a disliked being, past enemy or friend, future enemy or friend, present enemy or friend, a displeasing object, jealousy, habitual tendency, and disagreement with another's view. Aversion is likewise of ten forms, arising in sequence from these. Based on the first six grounds, nine vexations are established; aversion arising towards any of these is called aversion towards sentient beings.

items.zh: 餘名境界瞋；若不忍為先，亦有情瞋；若宿習瞋；若見瞋。

items.title: Section: Four Kinds of Aversion, and the Elder Who Chose Death Over an Unwinnable Argument

items.zh: 如是十瞋，略有三種。一、有情瞋，二、境界瞋，三、見瞋。
items.en: These ten forms of aversion may be briefly grouped into three: aversion towards beings, aversion towards objects, and aversion arising from views. Habitual aversion and view-based aversion each fall under whichever of these categories applies.

items.title: Section: Seven Grounds of Ignorance, Expanded to Nineteen — Not Knowing Where One Came From or Where One Is Going

items.zh: 無明依七事起。一、世事，二、世間安立事，三、運轉事，四、最勝事，五、真實事，六、雜染清淨事，七、增上慢事。依此七事，起七無知。或復十九。
items.en: Ignorance arises from seven grounds: temporal existence, the conventional structure of the world, cause and effect in motion, what is most excellent, what is genuinely real, defilement and purification, and presumptuous pride. From these seven grounds, seven forms of ignorance arise. These may also be expanded into nineteen.

items.zh: 當知於初事，由三種門生疑惑；於第二事，由內六處、若外、若俱，生我我所怨親等見；於第三事，由業、異熟及俱，生作者、受者、無因、惡因見；於第四事，誹謗三寶；於第五事，誹謗諸諦；於第六事，起邪解行；於第七事，依得自義起增上慢。

items.title: Section: Pride's Six Grounds Revisited — Why Two Distinct Kinds of Arrogance Share the Very Same Trigger

items.zh: 慢依六事生。一、劣有情，二、等有情，三、勝有情，四、內取蘊，五、已得未得顛倒，六、功德顛倒。依此六事，生七種慢。謂慢、過慢等。當知二慢依勝有情事生，餘各依一事。
items.en: Pride arises from six grounds: an inferior being, an equal being, a superior being, clinging to the aggregates as self, confused judgement about attainment, and confused judgement about merit. From these six grounds, seven kinds of pride arise: ordinary pride, excessive pride, and so on. One should know that two of these kinds of pride arise from the single ground of a superior being; each of the rest arises from its own single ground.

items.zh: 見依二事生。一、增益事，二、損減事。

items.title: Section: Wrong View's Two Directions — Affirming What Isn't There, Denying What Is

items.zh: 增益事有四種。一、我有性增益，二、常無常性增益，三、增上生方便增益，四、解脫方便增益。損減事亦有四種。一、謗因，二、謗果，三、謗作用，四、謗善事。當知此中，謂無施與乃至無妙行、惡行，是名謗因。謂無妙行、惡行業果異熟，是名謗果。謂無此世間乃至無化生有情，名謗作用。所以者何？諸士夫用是此中作用義。此士夫用復有四種。一、往來用，二、持胎藏用，三、置種子用，四、後有業用。若謂世間無阿羅漢等，名謗善事。依此廣略八事、二事，生於五見。謂薩迦耶見、邊執見、見取、戒禁取、邪見。又依六十二事，生邊執見及邪見。
items.en: Over-affirmation is of four kinds: affirming a real self, affirming permanence or its opposite, affirming a misguided means to higher rebirth, and affirming a mistaken means to liberation. Under-negation is likewise of four kinds: denying cause, denying effect, denying function, and denying wholesome activity. From these eight grounds broadly, or these two grounds briefly, five views arise: self-view, extreme view, view-attachment, precept-attachment, and wrong view. Depending further on sixty-two specific grounds, extreme view and wrong view arise in their full elaborated forms.

items.zh: 謂計前際事、計後際事，如經廣說。依此事差別，有六十二見。

items.title: Section: Six Ways Doubt Takes Hold — Completing the Grounds for All Six Root Afflictions

items.zh: 疑依六事生。一、聞不正法，二、見師邪行，三、見所信受意見差別，四、性自愚魯，五、甚深法性，六、廣大法教。
items.en: Doubt arises from six grounds: hearing false teaching, witnessing a teacher's improper conduct, finding one's own opinion at odds with that of those one trusts, one's own inherently dull disposition, reality's own profundity, and the vastness of the teaching.

items.title: Section: Fifteen Ways Affliction Differs — Inside the Six Gates, Outside Them, and Everywhere Between

items.zh: 答：一切差別，略有十五。一、內門煩惱，二、外門煩惱，三、見斷煩惱，四、修斷煩惱，五、可愛趣纏所攝煩惱，六、非可愛趣纏所攝煩惱，七、隨眠所攝煩惱，八、軟品煩惱，九、中品煩惱，十、上品煩惱，十一、散亂位煩惱，十二、諫悔位煩惱，十三、羸劣位煩惱，十四、制伏位煩惱，十五、離繫位煩惱。
items.en: Answer: all such distinctions may be briefly summarised as fifteen — affliction through the inner gates, through the outer gates, severed by insight, severed by cultivation, bound to a desirable destiny, bound to an undesirable destiny, subsumed under the latent seed, of soft grade, of medium grade, of superior grade, present in a scattered mind, present at admonition and confession, weakened through cultivation, suppressed through concentration, and finally severed from bondage.

items.title: Section: Using Craving to Sever Craving — Root Affliction's Final Angle, and Its Whole Nine-Part Analysis Complete

items.zh: 復次，煩惱無有功德，有多過失。謂於纏位污心相續，廣說如有尋有伺地。復次，煩惱非能對治。雖復經言：依愛斷愛、依慢斷慢。然非煩惱；但是善心加行希求高舉行相，與彼相似，假說愛、慢。復次，如前說十五種心對治差別，當知煩惱是彼所治，亦十五種。
items.en: Furthermore, affliction carries no benefit, only much fault. Furthermore, affliction cannot itself serve as a remedy. Though scripture speaks of using craving to sever craving, or pride to sever pride, this is not genuine affliction, but a wholesome state's own diligent, aspiring, upwards-striving character merely resembling it, borrowing the name by analogy. Furthermore, as already explained, the fifteen kinds of remedy correspond exactly to fifteen kinds of what they remedy — affliction itself.

blocks.text: Where each root affliction takes hold. Read it slowly as a mirror: each "ground" is a situation you will recognise.

Master Cháng Bǎi: recalling a lovely object enjoyed in the past, dwelling on its beauty, gives rise to the hindrance of sensual desire. Because the aggregates are not wholly suffering, sometimes pleasant, beings crave them.
Master Cháng Bǎi: the last three grounds each have lovable and unlovable sides, friend and enemy; with the first three, nine vexations.

Aversion towards beings, towards objects, and from views. Master Cháng Bǎi: seeds planted by frequent anger in past lives bring frequent anger now; whatever is done leaves a trace, and frequent anger now builds habit for the next life. (Untranslated, 0603b26: doubt arises in three ways about the past; views of self and other, friend and enemy, about the six sense bases; views of agent and experiencer about karma; and slander of the Three Jewels and the truths.)
Seven grounds, opened into nineteen. Master Cháng Bǎi: the first is ignorance about past, present, and future aggregates; the last, not truly knowing the fruits of the path.
Master Cháng Bǎi: thinking oneself better than one who is truly superior is "pride exceeding pride".
Four over-affirmations and four denials. Master Cháng Bǎi: one wrong view denies that human effort has any effect.
Master Cháng Bǎi: seeing that one's own view differs from what the teacher teaches, doubt arises.
Master Cháng Bǎi: desire-realm minds are scattered, so their afflictions arise at the sense gates.
"Using craving to sever craving" is not true affliction: a wholesome aspiration merely resembles it and borrows the name.
"Using craving to end craving": the wish for liberation looks like desire, but the treatise does not count it as affliction. Aspiration towards the good is part of the path.

quiz.q: The English has "covering craving" for 蓋貪. What is 蓋, according to the lecture?
options: it is the 蓋 of the five hindrances: recalling past enjoyment gives rise to the hindrance of desire or agitation; "covering" is merely literal
it means concealing: craving hidden from others, so "covering" is right, meaning secret craving with no outward sign
it means a lid: craving for a roof
it means a canopy: craving for carriages
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: recalling a lovely object enjoyed in the past, dwelling on its beautiful features, and giving rise to the hindrance of sensual desire or of agitation is called 蓋貪. So 蓋 is the technical term for the five hindrances. The English "covering craving" is literal; "hindrance-craving" would connect it to the familiar list.

quiz.q: Craving arises from ten grounds. How does Master Cháng Bǎi explain aggregates, evil conduct, and male and female?
options: the aggregates are wholly suffering, so beings wish to leave them; evil conduct repels; such marks turn one away, and none truly stirs craving
all three are fixed by past karma, unrelated to present mind
all three are craving found only in arhats
the aggregates at times have pleasure, so beings crave them; profit by evil conduct stirs craving; seeing male and female marks brings inverted notions and craving grows
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: because the aggregates are not wholly suffering, at times having pleasant feeling, beings crave them; gaining profit through evil conduct stirs craving; and ordinary beings, unknowing, seeing marks of male and female form inverted notions, so that craving arises and grows. The English "maleness and femaleness" is one of ten grounds, each with its matching name.

quiz.q: How are the nine vexations counted from the first six grounds?
options: each of the six across three times gives eighteen, half of which is nine, the result of reckoning by time
nine kinds of beings, each giving one vexation
one vexation for each of the nine attainments
the first three, plus the last three each divided into lovable and unlovable: three and six make nine
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi, following the Sub-commentary: the last three grounds each have lovable and unlovable, called friend and enemy, giving six, and with the first three there are nine. The English overview says three multiplied across three times; that does not match this account, and it miscounts the source of the nine.

quiz.q: Into what three are the ten aversions grouped, and where do habitual and view-based aversion fall?
options: of body, speech, and mind; habitual aversion is bodily and view-based verbal, for a view must be spoken
superior, medium, and soft aversion
of the desire, form, and formless realms
towards beings, towards objects, and from views; habitual and view-based aversion towards beings count as the first, towards disagreeable objects as the second
quiz.why: The treatise groups the ten into aversion towards beings, towards objects, and from views. Master Cháng Bǎi: aversion from the first six grounds and the eighth belongs to aversion towards beings; habitual and view-based aversion count as towards beings or objects according to what they arise on. The English closing clause states the Sub-commentary's point as if it were the treatise's.

quiz.q: What is habitual aversion, and what does Master Cháng Bǎi draw from it?
options: past anger infused seeds that stir frequent anger now; frequent anger now in turn builds habitual aversion for the next life
it comes from present surroundings, unrelated to the past, and vanishes on a change of place, needing no practice
it is hatred towards one's dwelling
it is a subtle aversion of noble ones alone
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: seeds infused by frequent anger in past lives cause frequent anger in this life; whatever is done leaves a trace, and frequent anger now builds up as habitual aversion for the next life. The point is practical: anger indulged today is the disposition of tomorrow.

quiz.q: From which seven grounds does ignorance arise?
options: form, feeling, perception, formations, consciousness, space, and analytical cessation
the seven limbs of awakening, ignorance being their reverse, so that its grounds are those limbs turned around
the seven prides, ignorance always arising from pride
temporal existence, the world's conventional structure, cause and effect in motion, the most excellent, the real, defilement and purification, and presumptuous pride
quiz.why: The treatise lists seven grounds, which may be opened into nineteen. Master Cháng Bǎi: the first is ignorance about the aggregates of past, present, and future; the last is not truly knowing the fruits of the path, thinking one has reached a state one has not. The English omits the passage matching the seven to the nineteen.

quiz.q: Which two of the seven prides arise from the ground of a superior being?
options: self-pride and presumptuous pride: taking aggregates as self; claiming what is unattained, both from comparing beings
pride exceeding pride and lowly pride: thinking oneself better than a superior, or only slightly below one far above
ordinary and excessive pride: better than the inferior; better than an equal
wrong pride and lowly pride: claiming virtue without it; thinking oneself low
quiz.why: The treatise says two kinds arise from a superior being, the others from one ground each. Master Cháng Bǎi: thinking oneself better than one who is truly superior is pride exceeding pride; thinking oneself only slightly below one far above is lowly pride. Pride regarding the aggregates is self-pride, on which all the rest depend.

quiz.q: What are the four over-affirmations and the four under-negations?
options: affirming a self, permanence or its opposite, means to higher rebirth, means to liberation; denying cause, effect, function, and wholesome activity
affirming denial of cause, effect, function, and good; negating a self, permanence, and the means to rebirth and to liberation
adding craving, aversion, ignorance, and pride; reducing faith, diligence, mindfulness, and concentration, so afflictions rise and good declines
adding the four aggregates; reducing the four qualities of nirvāṇa
quiz.why: The treatise lists four over-affirmations and four under-negations, from which the five views arise. Master Cháng Bǎi: taking the selfless aggregates as self gives the view of self; regarding what cannot bring liberation as doing so is over-affirming a means to liberation. So wrong view is both adding what is not there and denying what is.

quiz.q: The English has "denying function" for 謗作用. How does the lecture explain this 作用?
options: 作用 means the Buddha's powers, so it is denying miracles, and "function" should be "miracles," nothing to do with persons
作用 means the elements' functions, so "function" is exact
作用 refers specifically to human agency, a person's doing; "function" is too general and loses this
作用 means the work of mental factors, and should be "mental function"
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: this is 士夫用; 士夫 means a person, and a person's doing is the meaning of 作用 here. So the wrong view denies that human effort has any effect. The English "function" is correct as a dictionary word, but a reader would not guess the specific sense intended.

quiz.q: The English has "differing opinions among the trusted" for 見所信受意見差別. Whose opinions differ?
options: one's own view differs from one's teacher's or the trusted teaching, and doubt arises; the English makes it a difference among the trusted
the Buddha and great disciples disagree, so "among the trusted" is right, noble ones also differing
laity and monastics disagree
different schools' doctrines differ
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: seeing that one's own view differs from what the teacher teaches, doubt about what one has learned arises. So the difference lies between the learner and what the learner trusts. The English "differing opinions among the trusted" shifts the disagreement into the group of trusted authorities, which the Chinese does not require.

quiz.q: What are inner-gate afflictions, and those of the scattered and suppressed stages?
options: discrimination from faculties meeting objects is inner-gate; the desire realm's scattered mind is scattered stage; those to be subdued for absorption are suppressed stage
inner-gate belongs to monastics and outer-gate to laity; scattered stage is in the form realm, suppressed in the formless, neither in the desire realm
inner-gate is bodily illness; scattered is walking; suppressed is being arrested
inner-gate is the store-consciousness; scattered is manas; suppressed is mental consciousness
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: afflictions from false discrimination, arising as faculties take objects and consciousness is born, are inner-gate afflictions; desire-realm beings have scattered minds without absorption, and so their afflictions are of the scattered stage; those that must be subdued in order to gain absorption are of the suppressed stage.

quiz.q: Scripture speaks of using craving to sever craving. Can affliction remedy affliction?
options: yes: a great craving can overpower a small one, so affliction truly remedies affliction, and even pride helps when well used
yes, but only noble ones can do so
no: wholesome effort's aspiring, uplifted aspect merely resembles them and borrows the names; only differing natures can remedy
no: this scripture is spurious, and the treatise rejects its source
quiz.why: The treatise says this is not genuine affliction; a wholesome state's aspiring and uplifted character merely resembles it and borrows the name. Master Cháng Bǎi: wholesome aspiration belongs to the good, and the desire severed to the unwholesome; only because they differ in nature is there remedy. Good cures evil.
